doc.title: Frank Alkyer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Orleans, Louisiana, January 10, 2020

chapter: Remembering writers and stories behind the magazine
title: Nat Hentoff and letting the artist speak
summary: Alkyer praises Hentoff's writing, which he first read at the Village Voice, and the practice of quoting artists directly. He recalls working with Hentoff on book projects.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Did you have a good relationship with Nat Hentoff? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Yeah, I did. But I always wanted him — his time at DownBeat I don’t think ended well back in the 50s, which is a recurring theme. I like to think it hasn’t happened as often under my tenure there. But there were turf wars, there were people, but Nat Hentoff, I started reading Nat Hentoff not necessarily in DownBeat but when I lived in New York and the Village Voice when he was covering the Supreme Court. And I loved his writing. You know the Village Voice was my paper in New York City. That was the thing that I ran to every Thursday and bought for a buck and read it cover to cover because it was covering the things that I wanted to see. And Nat Hentoff was one of them. And he was just heroic to me. And he was one of those guys too, it’s like okay after I learned about it, this was like when I was 22, 21, 23 maybe, when I got to New York. So I went back and started looking up Nat Hentoff things, go to the library and look up old DownBeats. It’s like I heard — and read it — and still to this day his writing going back to your point about writing about music, what he did was ingenious and right, that he would let the artist speak. So as a result of people like Bill Gottlieb and Nat Hentoff and Dan Morgenstern that the artists’ voice is front and center in those pieces, most of those pieces. Instead of having a critic that would just wax eloquently for 2000 words about an artist and never quote them. That doesn’t have a lot of lasting value. It’s interesting. But those direct interviews with those artists capturing what they are thinking at the time are gold. They’re just so inspiring. But you were asking about Nat. Sorry.

Yeah, no. We got to know him a little bit. I did an interview with him and it was a challenge. Not ‘cause he was — he was very nice. But he was Nat Hentoff. And I felt like everything I’m asking him I hope is not like silly.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. He was a good guy. But I think he was kind of like, you know, but we worked on a couple of projects. It’s like he would call up, “Hey Frank I’m putting together a book can I get” — because we owned the rights to those articles. I said of course. And for those people we would just say yeah, those are your articles, you have the right to do that. There’s no charge for that. So we would work together on things like that. And when there was an anniversary issue we had us write some pieces for us. Yeah, yeah. And it was great. I was never happier than when a Nat Hentoff piece would run in DownBeat magazine.
